Ferrari Goes Old-School ICE Cool, Releases Twin 296 Challenge Stradale, Evo With 670+ HP Turbo Magic
74 photos
Photo: Ferrari
Just two days after GTA VI hit consoles, Maranello rolled out a pair of track-bred machines that look like they landed straight from the video game onto real asphalt. With towering fixed wings, aggressive front splitters, and stripped-back carbon-fiber bodywork, the 296 Challenge Stradale and 296 Challenge EVO pack the unmistakable visual punch of maxed-out Vice City supercars. The only difference is that neither needs a controller, an online lobby, or a cheat code to shred a real racetrack.
Ferrari unveiled the twins at the Finali Mondiali at the Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya in Montmeló. Developed side by side, both cars pack a the three-liter, 120-degree twin-turbocharged V6 from the 296 GTB, but stripped of the hybrid bloatware. Both weigh 1.3 tons / 3,000 lb dry, and they represent Ferrari taking a big step back.
Not mechanically or technologically, but conceptually, putting grip and featherweight body mass ahead of electrification in both the road car and its track-only alter ego (Alter Evo?).
The 296 Challenge Stradale revives the nameplate last seen on the 360 Challenge Stradale in 2003, as Ferrari's most track-focused road car. Its mid-mounted, hot-V twin-turbo V6 produces 670 PS / 661 hp at 8,000 rpm and 740 Nm / 546 lb-ft of torque at 6,250 rpm with an 8,500 rpm redline. Revised boost control and variable valve timing lift dynamic torque by over 32% compared with the 296 GTB.
Photo: Ferrari Removing the battery and electric motor trims 140 kg / 309 lb compared with the 296 GTB, bringing dry weight to 1,330 kg / 2,932 lb. That yields a power-to-weight ratio of 497 bhp/metric ton. Race-derived hardware includes insulated turbochargers, Formula 1 knock-control software, a lighter flexplate, a Belt Starter Generator, and larger twin tailpipes, paired with an 8-speed dual-clutch gearbox mixing 296 Challenge logic with SF90 XX Stradale-derived 250-millisecond shifts.
Ferrari quotes 0 to 100 kph (62 mph), in 2.8 seconds, 0 to 200 kph/124 mph, in 7.9 seconds, and a top speed above 300 kph, or 186 mph. Braking from 200 kph takes 101 meters / 331 feet, and the checkered flag at Fiorano falls 1 minute and 18.5 seconds after start. Its fixed wing , splitter, flicks, aero damper, vortex generators, and enclosed underbody generate 617 kg / 1,360 lb of downforce at 250 kph (155 mph), up 72% from the standard 296 GTB.
Beneath the stripped-back bodywork, mechanical grip receives an equally serious upgrade. More aggressive suspension geometry works with adaptive dampers and springs over twice as stiff as previous road setups, paired with bespoke Pirelli P Zero R or P Zero Trofeo RS tires. ABS Evo operates across every Manettino mode and road condition, assisted by the F80 hypercar's Ferrari Integrated Vehicle Estimator to keep rear-wheel traction predictable when drivers push hard at the limit.
Photo: Ferrari Inside, the cabin discards everyday padding for tubular racing seats, technical fabrics, and single-piece carbon-fiber door panels stripped of armrests and storage pockets. Engineers also redesigned the center console and floor mats to shave further weight, while recalibrating the cabin sound system to balance intake and exhaust noise all the way to 8,500 rpm.
Despite that raw track-day specification, Ferrari still includes its standard 7-year maintenance program for every road-going buyer. For those who don’t like two-way lanes or traffic stops, the Evo is the alternative.
Built strictly for circuit competition, the 296 Challenge Evo is the tenth Challenge model in the Prancing Horse’s single-marque series established in 1993, debuting in the 2027 European and North American seasons. Its non-hybrid 3.0-liter V6 delivers 700 PS / 690 hp at 7,500 rpm, equaling 234 PS / 231 hp per liter, alongside 740 Nm / 546 lb-ft and an 8,500-rpm limit. With a seven-speed gearbox and the same 1,330 kg / 2,932 lb dry weight, it achieves 519 bhp/ton.
Photo: Ferrari Aerodynamics represent the biggest leap over the outgoing 296 Challenge, bringing the racer's balance closer to the 296 GT3 Evo. A reshaped underbody, revised splitter-to-floor transition, three pairs of front vortex generators, and two rear pairs lift peak downforce by 12%, adding roughly 100 kg / 220 lb at 250 kph/155 mph. Teams can switch between a High Downforce setup for technical circuits and a new Low Drag kit cutting minimum drag by 4%.
The aerodynamic load spread between those two configurations has more than doubled, letting engineers tailor balance across vastly different tracks. A wider rear-wing adjustment range, redesigned rear diffuser, revised mirrors, and added carbon-fiber components expand that setup window further. Raising rear ride height by up to 10 mm / 0.39 inches unlocks roughly 30 kg / 66 lb of extra downforce at 250 kph, while a cooled high-performance driveshaft handles sustained race loads.
Electronic updates target stability and cornering speed for both experienced amateur racers and younger circuit drivers. Reworked traction-control strategies and an upgraded electronic differential sharpen high-speed agility and braking poise across rapid direction changes. Carbon-ceramic CCM-R brakes work with a new pedal curve that increases modulation, travel, and pedal effort for the same deceleration.
Photo: Ferrari On the steering wheel, the Manettino provides four ABS calibrations tuned for dry or wet asphalt, balancing speed and stability.
In comparative track testing , the 296 Challenge Evo reduced tire wear and shaved 0.8 seconds per lap off the previous 296 Challenge at Mugello. A redesigned instrument cluster displays control intervention levels, tire-pressure data, and lap times more clearly during stints. Those upgrades prepare teams for the 2027 Ferrari Challenge calendar, which adds three 40-minute, two-driver endurance races featuring a mandatory pit stop, beginning with the season's second round at Mugello.
